summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free, single-file web app that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Pick a site (South Pole reference points near the Artemis candidate regions, CLPS and international landers, Apollo sites, or any custom coordinates) and a landing date. The app shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the local horizon, how much a vertical solar array would produce, how long until sunset or Earthset, and when direct-to-Earth communication is possible. A 360-degree horizon view, an animated timeline, a side-by-side comparison of up to eight sites, and a landing-date finder that scans 12 months for opportunities meeting power and communication constraints turn complex ephemeris geometry into quick, clear decisions. Positions agree with NASA/JPL DE421 to better than 0.1 arcminute. When launches slip or sites change, teams can find the next viable window instantly, and students can see why the lunar south pole is so challenging.
details: WHAT IT DOES Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers the two questions that decide whether a lunar surface mission can work at a given place and time: Will the Sun be above my horizon (power and thermal)? Will Earth be above my horizon (direct-to-Earth communications)? Users choose a site and a landing date and immediately see: - Live metrics: Sun elevation and azimuth, visible Sun-disk fraction, solar array output for a vertical sun-tracking array, time to sunset or sunrise, Earth elevation and azimuth, direct-to-Earth link status, time to Earthset or Earthrise, and window statistics (percent sunlit, longest darkness, percent Earth in view, longest comms blackout). - Horizon view: a 360-degree panorama from the site showing the Sun and Earth now, plus their paths over the analysis window. At the south pole you can watch the Sun circle the horizon and Earth trace its libration loop up and down through the horizon. - Timeline and animation: Sun and Earth elevation relative to the local horizon over 14 days to 1 year, with lit and comms windows shaded. Click to jump in time or press Play. - Compare sites: up to 8 sites side by side, with colour-coded availability strips (Sun, Earth, both) and a sortable table with an adjustable power/comms weighted score. - Landing-date finder: for example, 'I need 7 days of continuous sunlight after landing and Earth in view at least 50 percent of that time.' The finder scans the next 12 months and lists every opportunity; one click re-runs the analysis for that date. This directly supports re-planning when launches slip. - Terrain inputs: height above surroundings (the horizon dips on the curved, airless Moon: 1 km up gives about 1.9 degrees, 6 km gives about 4.8 degrees), a uniform horizon elevation, or a pasted azimuth:elevation horizon mask (for example, derived from LOLA topography in LROC QuickMap). - CSV export of the full time series, and a 'How it works' explainer for students and the public. SITE LIBRARY Reference points near the Artemis south-polar candidate regions (Shackleton-de Gerlache Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Nobile, Mons Mouton, Cabeus, plus the Shackleton floor as a permanently shadowed example); CLPS and international landers (IM-1 Odysseus, IM-2 Athena, Blue Ghost M1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e 4, Chang'e 6); Apollo 11-17; and any custom latitude/longitude. HOW IT WORKS For each time step we compute geocentric Sun and Moon vectors (J2000), rotate them into the Moon body-fixed frame with the IAU/WGCCRE lunar rotation model (including physical libration terms), and convert to topocentric azimuth and elevation at the site. This includes surface parallax (about 0.26 degrees for Earth) and the angular size of the Sun's disk. Each position is then compared with the local horizon. The Sun counts as lit when at least half its disk is visible; comms are available when Earth's centre is above the horizon plus a user-set margin. ACCURACY We validated the app against NASA/JPL DE421 using Skyfield and an independent implementation of the IAU rotation model: 200 samples, 5 sites, about 1 year. Maximum differences in Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation are below 0.1 arcminute. A full lunar day for 6 sites computes in under 0.2 s in the browser. TOOLS JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas and CSS, packaged as one self-contained HTML file that works offline with no install; the Astronomy Engine library (MIT); Python, Skyfield and DE421 for validation; Playwright and headless Chrome for testing and screenshots. BENEFITS AND IMPACT Planners can make fast what-if trades across sites and dates when constraints change, and science and engineering teams share one clear picture of power and comms windows. Educators and the public see why the lunar south pole is so different: a Sun that grazes the horizon, an Earth that bobs above and below it, and how a few hundred metres of height can turn darkness into sunlight. CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES We chose a human-eye horizon panorama over abstract tables, availability strips that compare many sites at a glance, and a constraint-based landing-date finder instead of manual date hunting. We also report power for a vertical tracking array, because at the poles whether the Sun's disk clears the horizon matters far more than how high it is. LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS Without a horizon mask, terrain is idealised as a smooth sphere, so results are best case. Site coordinates are approximate reference points, not official mission sites. Next steps: automatic LOLA DEM horizon masks, relay-orbiter coverage, a 3D surface view and thermal (shadow-hours) metrics. AI DISCLOSURE Source code, README and slide text were written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), a generative AI assistant, and reviewed by our team. This is disclosed in the app footer, the HTML metadata, the README and the demo deck. No AI-generated images and no NASA logos or branding are used.
